findings.evidence: Gap 1 {price, charge, toll, cost}: ‘toll’ is the member whose dominant figurative sense (damage, casualties) sits outside the price/cost/charge cluster — key C. Gap 2 {relaxed, spirited, amused, pointed}: on valence, ‘pointed’ is the only critically-charged member against three positives — key D. Gap 4 {Similarly, Eventually, Presumably, Ironically}: ‘Eventually’ is the only pure temporal adverb against three stance/comment adverbs — key B. Gap 3 {ground, field, horse, floor} breaks the pattern cleanly: the marked member is ‘horse’ (the only non-surface) and the key is ‘ground’. findings.claim: The gap-4 rationale dismisses its strongest rival on the wrong clause: it refutes ‘Ironically’ against the main proposition only, and does not engage the irony that is actually available in the appositive.
findings.evidence: Rationale as shipped: “Ironically = wrong_logic: someone finally yielding is exactly what the whole paragraph has led the reader to expect, and an expected outcome cannot be ironic.” The gapped sentence is “___(4)___, somebody cracks – nearly always the same somebody, the one who minds the mess a little more than the rest and minds it first.” G-KEY-relegB independently named this the live rival: “D ‘Ironically’ is the strongest rival — there is mild irony in the most fastidious person doing the work — but it leaves ‘the kitchen waits’ hanging with no resolution in time.”
findings.why: The rationale’s premise is true of the main clause — somebody cracking is the expected end of the escalation — but the appositive supplies a textbook situational irony the rationale never addresses: the person who minds the mess most is the one who pays for everyone else’s not minding it. A student who spots that will find the shipped rationale answering a point they did not make. The generalisation “an expected outcome cannot be ironic” is also stated more absolutely than it holds (dramatic irony is built on expected outcomes); the intended and correct sense is situational irony.

Both fresh relegation legs and both fleet legs committed to B, and this audit’s cold solve reached B on the same discharge argument before reading any rationale. The teaching payload would be stronger if the D entry conceded the appositive irony and then refuted it on scope — ‘the irony, such as it is, is in who cracks, not in that somebody does; the connective governs the main clause’. findings.claim: The gap-5 rationale’s dismissal of ‘cast’ is a shade stronger than the historical record supports: it says “a real idiom family, but nothing with ‘balance’”, and there is in fact an attested ‘cast a balance’.
findings.evidence: ‘Cast’ in the sense ‘add up, reckon (accounts)’ is a genuine (archaic/technical bookkeeping) sense — ‘cast up one’s accounts’, ‘cross-cast’, and ‘cast the balance’ attested from the seventeenth century; checked externally rather than asserted. The frame, however, is “most kitchens ___ an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor, held in place by whoever has stopped expecting credit”.
findings.why: The archaism does not reach the frame, on three independent grounds, which is why this is info and not a second-defensible-answer finding: (i) it requires the LEDGER sense of ‘balance’ — a computed figure — whereas the passage’s balance is an equilibrium, and the phrase ‘between confrontation and squalor’ fixes it as such; (ii) the surviving modern form is ‘cast up’, not bare ‘cast’; (iii) the register is dead prose and this is a contemporary BrE working-life column, so no solver reaches it. Recorded only so that the rationale’s absolute ‘nothing with balance’ is not mistaken for a lexicographic fact.
